Week 5 Overview

The Shift in Purpose

Weeks 1–4 built your structural and procedural knowledge of TOGAF. You can now navigate every ADM phase, explain every governance mechanism, name every artifact type, and understand the Enterprise Continuum. That is roughly 60–65% of what the exam tests.

Week 5 targets the remaining 35–40%: applied knowledge.

The TOGAF Level 1 exam has two distinct question styles:

  1. Recall questions — "What does Phase X produce?" "Which document is created in Phase F?" "What are the two continua?" These reward knowledge.
  2. Scenario questions — "An organization has [situation described in plain language]. Which TOGAF concept applies?" These reward understanding and recognition.

Scenario questions are harder because TOGAF terminology never appears in the problem — only in the answer choices. You must recognize a TOGAF concept operating in the real world without being told what it is. The five skills scenario questions test:

  • Domain recognition: Which architecture domain owns this problem?
  • Phase recognition: Which ADM phase is operating here?
  • Artifact selection: Which artifact captures this information?
  • Concept matching: Which TOGAF concept describes this situation?
  • Framework integration: Which complementary framework supports this activity?

Week 5 builds all five skills deliberately.

What This Week Does NOT Repeat

The following topics were covered in depth in prior weeks and will not be re-explained here. Week 5 references them but assumes you know them:

Topic Covered In

Day 1 (Monday): Business Architecture — Applied Domain Deep Dive

Where Business Architecture Sits in the ADM

Business Architecture is produced in Phase B. It is the first domain-level architecture developed after Architecture Vision (Phase A) is approved. Everything built in Phases C and D must trace back to it. This makes Business Architecture the root of all architecture decisions.

The formal purpose of Phase B: describe the baseline and target Business Architecture in sufficient detail to allow the architecture team to identify the right data, application, and technology changes needed to achieve the business vision.

The Business Architecture's Four Concerns

Phase B answers four questions in precise TOGAF terms:

Question TOGAF Concept What It Produces
What does the organization DO? Business Capabilities Business Capability Map
How does the organization DO it? Business Processes and Functions Process flows, function decomposition
Who does what? Roles, Actors, Organizational Units Org Map, Actor/Role Catalog
Why is the organization doing this? Business Goals and Objectives Business Motivation Model

Understanding this four-part structure is critical for scenario questions: when a scenario says "the architect is identifying which capabilities need to change," that is Phase B — Business Architecture, capability analysis. When it says "the architect is documenting who approves decisions," that is Phase B — roles and actors.

Business Motivation Model (BMM) — Full Coverage

The Business Motivation Model is a standard (from OMG — Object Management Group) that TOGAF adopts to connect business strategy to architecture. It organizes motivation into two tracks: Ends (where the organization is going) and Means (how it will get there). Both tracks are influenced by external and internal Influencers.

The Ends Hierarchy (Most Abstract → Most Concrete)

VISION
  │
  ├── GOAL (qualitative desired results supporting the Vision)
  │     │
  │     └── OBJECTIVE (SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound)
  • Vision: The aspirational future state. Long-term, inspirational, qualitative. Example: "Be the leading digital bank in the GCC by 2030."
  • Goal: A broad desired result in support of the Vision. Still qualitative. Example: "Improve customer digital experience." Multiple Goals support one Vision.
  • Objective: A SMART (measurable, time-bound) target supporting a Goal. Example: "Increase mobile app daily active users by 40% by December 2026." Multiple Objectives support one Goal.

The Means Hierarchy (Most Abstract → Most Concrete)

MISSION
  │
  ├── STRATEGY (broad approach for achieving Goals)
  │     │
  │     └── TACTIC (specific action implementing a Strategy)
  • Mission: What the organization does — its fundamental activity. Example: "Provide accessible, innovative financial services to retail and SME customers."
  • Strategy: A broad approach chosen to achieve a specific Goal. Example: "Invest in mobile-first customer experiences." Multiple Strategies support Goals.
  • Tactic: A specific, concrete action implementing a Strategy. Example: "Launch a redesigned mobile app by Q3 2026." Multiple Tactics implement one Strategy.

Influencers

Influencers are internal or external factors that affect the organization and therefore shape its Ends and Means:

  • External: Competition, regulation, technology change, market trends, economic conditions
  • Internal: Culture, existing capabilities, available budget, leadership priorities

Influencers drive Assessments — analyses of how the influencer affects the organization. Assessments identify Risks and Opportunities that feed into SWOT analyses.

BMM and TOGAF — The Connection

The BMM is NOT a deliverable you produce from scratch in every ADM cycle. It is a conceptual model that helps architects:

  1. Understand the business motivation BEFORE designing architecture
  2. Ensure architecture decisions trace to business Goals and Objectives
  3. Identify what capabilities and processes must change to achieve the Objectives

In Phase A, the Architect uses BMM thinking to create the Architecture Vision — the high-level statement of what the target architecture will achieve and why. In Phase B, the BMM underpins the full Business Architecture by connecting capabilities to Goals and Objectives.

Exam tip

Know the BMM hierarchy direction: Vision → Goal → Objective (Ends, most abstract to most concrete); Mission → Strategy → Tactic (Means, most abstract to most concrete). A question might describe a "time-bound measurable target" → Objective, not Goal. Or "a broad desired result" → Goal, not Objective.

Business Capabilities vs. Business Functions vs. Business Processes

This is one of the most frequently tested distinctions in the Business Architecture section. The three concepts are related but operate at different levels of abstraction:

Concept Level Stability What It Answers Example
Business Capability Strategic Very stable (years) WHAT the organization can do "Customer Onboarding Capability"
Business Function Operational (grouping) Stable (months–years) WHAT activity grouping exists "Customer Identity Verification Function"
Business Process Operational (flow) Changes often HOW an activity is performed step-by-step "KYC Document Verification Process"

Business Capability:

  • Describes WHAT the organization is able to do at a strategic level
  • Stable: Capabilities don't change when processes are reorganized
  • Does NOT describe HOW something is done
  • Expressed as nouns: "Customer Relationship Management," "Product Innovation," "Supply Chain Execution"
  • The Business Capability Map organizes capabilities in a hierarchy (Level 1 → Level 2 → Level 3)

Business Function:

  • A grouping of related activities that produces a specific output
  • Falls between Capability (strategic) and Process (operational)
  • A capability may decompose into several functions
  • Example: The "Customer Onboarding" capability may include functions: "Identity Verification," "Account Setup," "Welcome Communication"

Business Process:

  • A specific, sequential set of activities performed to achieve a defined outcome
  • Has a trigger, a sequence of steps, decision points, and an output
  • HOW a function is performed
  • Modeled using BPMN (Business Process Model and Notation)
  • Changes frequently as the organization improves or reorganizes
Exam tip

A scenario saying "a stable, strategically defined ability to perform X" → Business Capability. A scenario saying "the step-by-step flow for processing a customer complaint" → Business Process. A scenario saying "the grouping of all activities related to financial reporting" → Business Function. Don't confuse the three — they appear in different artifacts and at different levels.

Value Chain vs. Value Stream — The Critical Distinction

These two concepts describe business value creation at different levels:

Value Chain (Porter's Model):

  • A HIGH-LEVEL conceptual model showing ALL categories of activities that create value for an organization
  • Generic — the same Value Chain structure applies to any organization in the same industry
  • Does NOT show sequence of specific steps; shows CATEGORIES of activity
  • Porter's Value Chain: Primary Activities (Inbound Logistics, Operations, Outbound Logistics, Marketing & Sales, Service) + Support Activities (Infrastructure, HR, Technology, Procurement)
  • Used in Phase B to understand how the organization creates value at a strategic level

Value Stream:

  • A SPECIFIC, end-to-end sequence of activities delivering value to a SPECIFIC stakeholder for a SPECIFIC outcome
  • Shows every step, handoff, wait time, and decision from trigger to value delivery
  • Specific — each Value Stream is unique to that stakeholder and outcome
  • Example: "New Business Customer Onboarding Value Stream" — from first contact to first transaction, showing every step, who does it, and elapsed time
  • Used in Phase B to identify waste, bottlenecks, and optimization opportunities
Value Chain:
  [Support: Infrastructure | HR | Technology | Procurement]
  [Primary: Inbound → Operations → Outbound → Marketing → Service]
  ↑ Generic categories; applies to all organizations in the sector

Value Stream:
  Trigger → Step A → Handoff → Step B → Decision → Step C → Value Delivered
  ↑ Specific to one outcome for one stakeholder; this exact flow, this organization
Exam tip

Value Chain = Porter's strategic model, generic categories, high level. Value Stream = specific operational flow, one outcome, one stakeholder, shows all steps. They are NOT the same. A scenario describing "a generic model showing categories of activities from raw material to customer delivery" → Value Chain. A scenario describing "the specific sequence of steps from customer application to loan approval, including all handoffs" → Value Stream.

BPMN — Business Process Model and Notation (Exam-Relevant Elements)

BPMN is the standard notation for modeling Business Processes in Phase B. You do not need to be a BPMN expert for TOGAF Level 1, but you must know the key elements and their meanings because exam scenarios may present BPMN concepts.

Core BPMN Elements

Flow Objects:

Element Symbol Meaning
Start Event Circle (thin border) Where the process begins
Intermediate Event Circle (double border) Something that happens during the process
End Event Circle (thick border) Where the process ends
Task/Activity Rectangle (rounded corners) A unit of work performed
Subprocess Rectangle with + sign A task that contains its own internal process
Exclusive Gateway (XOR) Diamond with X One path taken; decision point
Parallel Gateway (AND) Diamond with + All paths taken simultaneously
Inclusive Gateway (OR) Diamond with O One or more paths taken

Swim Lanes (Pools and Lanes):

  • Pool: Represents a separate participant (organization, system, or external entity). Processes within one Pool are controlled by that participant.
  • Lane: A subdivision within a Pool representing a role or department. Activities in a Lane are performed by that role.

Flows:

  • Sequence Flow (solid arrow): Shows the order of activities within a Pool. Only connects objects within the same Pool.
  • Message Flow (dashed arrow): Shows communication between two separate Pools (two different participants). Cannot be used within the same Pool.
  • Data Association (dotted arrow): Connects a Data Object or Data Store to an activity.
Exam tip

The most commonly tested BPMN element is the distinction between Sequence Flow (within a Pool, solid) and Message Flow (between Pools, dashed). A scenario showing communication between a supplier and a purchasing department — if they are in separate Pools — uses Message Flow, not Sequence Flow.

Business Architecture Artifacts — Full Classification

Phase B produces three types of artifacts: Catalogs, Matrices, and Diagrams.

Catalogs (Inventories)

Catalog What It Lists
Organization/Actor Catalog All organizational units and named roles in the enterprise
Driver/Goal/Objective Catalog Business Drivers, Goals, and Objectives (from BMM)
Role Catalog All roles (human and system) with their responsibilities
Business Service/Function Catalog All business services and the functions that deliver them
Location Catalog All locations where business operates (buildings, regions, countries)
Process/Event/Control/Product Catalog Business processes, triggering events, controls, and outputs

Matrices (Cross-Reference Tables)

Matrix What It Shows Why It Matters
Business Interaction Matrix How organizational units interact with each other Identifies collaboration dependencies
Actor/Role Matrix Which actors can play which roles Governance; separation of duties analysis
Business Function/Organization Matrix Which org units perform which functions Identifies duplication; consolidation opportunities
Process/Event/Control/Product Matrix Processes triggered by events; controls applied; products output Compliance and control coverage

Diagrams (Visual Models)

Diagram What It Shows
Business Footprint Diagram How business goals, functions, services, and processes connect — the "why architecture exists" view
Business Service/Information Diagram Business services and the information they consume and produce
Functional Decomposition Diagram How business functions decompose into sub-functions (hierarchy)
Product Lifecycle Diagram How products evolve from introduction through retirement
Goal/Objective/Service Diagram Traceability from Goals and Objectives to Services that fulfill them
Business Capability Map All business capabilities organized in a hierarchy
Value Stream Map End-to-end activity sequence for a specific value delivery
Organizational Map Reporting structure, locations, inter-unit relationships
Process Flow Diagram (BPMN) Step-by-step business process with events, tasks, decisions, and actors
Actor Co-operation Diagram How actors collaborate to deliver a business service
Exam tip

The Business Footprint Diagram is unique to Phase B — it is the diagram that connects business drivers (Goals and Objectives) to organizational units to business functions to business services. It is the "why architecture exists" diagram. Do not confuse it with the Organizational Map (which shows reporting structure only) or the Capability Map (which shows capabilities only).

Gap Analysis in Business Architecture — How It Works in Practice

Gap Analysis in Phase B follows the same structure as all ADM Phases (see Week 2), but the gaps are specific to the business domain:

Business Architecture Gap Categories:

Gap Type Description Example
Capability Gap A business capability required in the Target Architecture that does not exist today "Real-time fraud detection capability does not exist; must be created"
Process Gap A business process that must change or be created "Current loan approval process takes 10 days; target requires 24 hours"
Role Gap A role required in the Target Architecture that does not exist "Digital Product Owner role does not exist in current org structure"
Service Gap A business service not currently offered "Self-service account opening not available in current state"
Eliminated Element Capability, function, or process in the baseline that should not exist in the target "Manual reconciliation process to be eliminated after ERP upgrade"

Gap Analysis produces a Gap Analysis Matrix that feeds directly into Phase E (Opportunities & Solutions) where gaps become Work Packages.

Key Takeaway for Day 1 (Business Architecture)

Business Architecture (Phase B) works at three levels: strategic (BMM, capabilities), operational (functions, services), and process (BPMN flows). Know the hierarchy: Vision → Goal → Objective (Ends); Mission → Strategy → Tactic (Means). Distinguish Capability (WHAT, stable, strategic) from Function (grouping, operational) from Process (HOW, sequential, changeable). Distinguish Value Chain (Porter's generic categories) from Value Stream (specific end-to-end delivery sequence for one stakeholder). The Business Footprint Diagram is the unique Phase B artifact that traces business drivers to services. Gap Analysis produces Capability/Process/Role/Service gaps that become Work Packages in Phase E.

Day 2 (Tuesday): Data Architecture — Applied Domain Deep Dive

Where Data Architecture Sits in the ADM

Data Architecture is the first sub-phase of Phase C (Information Systems Architecture). It is always done BEFORE Application Architecture because applications must be designed to handle the data — not the other way around.

The formal purpose: describe the structure of the organization's logical and physical data assets and associated data management resources in the Target Architecture, and identify the gaps from the Baseline Architecture.

Phase C Data Architecture answers:

  • What data entities exist and how are they related? (Logical data model)
  • How does data move through the enterprise? (Data flows)
  • Who is responsible for which data? (Data governance integration)
  • What are the data quality requirements? (Quality dimensions)
  • Which data is authoritative, and where? (Master Data Management)

Logical vs. Physical Data Architecture

Level What It Shows When Produced Example
Conceptual High-level entities and their relationships; no attributes Early Phase C "Customer has many Accounts"
Logical Entities, attributes, relationships, normalized; technology-independent Phase C core deliverable ERD with Customer(CustomerID, Name, Email) related to Account(AccountID, Balance)
Physical Actual database tables, columns, data types, indexes; technology-specific Phase D or implementation Oracle table CUSTOMER with columns CUST_ID VARCHAR2(36) PK...

For the TOGAF exam, the most important distinction is Logical vs. Physical:

  • Logical Data Architecture = technology-independent description of what data exists and how it relates. The domain of Phase C.
  • Physical Data Architecture = how data is stored in specific technologies. Begins to emerge in Phase D (Technology Architecture) when platforms are chosen.

Data Quality Dimensions — The Six Dimensions

Data quality is a core Phase C concern. TOGAF references data quality requirements in the Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS). There are six standard dimensions:

Dimension Definition Violation Example
Accuracy Data correctly represents the real-world entity it describes Customer address stored as "123 Main St" but actual address is "456 Oak Ave"
Completeness All required data is present; no mandatory fields are missing Customer record with no phone number or email
Consistency The same data appears the same way across all systems that store it Product named "Widget 5000" in ERP but "Widget-5000 Series" in CRM
Timeliness Data is available when needed and is sufficiently current Yesterday's stock price used for today's trading decisions
Validity Data conforms to defined formats, ranges, and business rules Date of birth recorded as "32/13/1985" (invalid date)
Uniqueness Each real-world entity is represented only once; no duplicates Two Customer records for the same person with slightly different names

How these dimensions appear in TOGAF:

  • They are stated as requirements in the Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS) — "Customer email must be 100% complete; Customer address must be validated against national address database (Validity)"
  • They feed into the Data Quality Requirements Matrix (Phase C artifact)
  • Violations found in Gap Analysis become remediation Work Packages in Phase E
Exam tip

The six dimensions appear in scenario questions as plain-language descriptions. "Missing required fields" → Completeness. "The same customer appears twice with different spellings" → Uniqueness. "The same data looks different in two systems" → Consistency. "The data is correct but from last week" → Timeliness. "The value doesn't match the allowed format" → Validity.

Canonical Data Model (CDM)

Problem it solves: When N enterprise systems each use their own format for representing a shared data entity (e.g., "Customer"), integrating them requires N × (N−1) / 2 bilateral transformations. For 10 systems that means 45 transformations; for 20 systems that means 190 transformations. Each transformation must be maintained when either system changes.

Solution — the Canonical Data Model: A single, enterprise-agreed representation of a data entity that ALL systems use when exchanging that entity. Systems transform their internal format to/from the canonical format once, reducing N × (N−1) / 2 transformations to just N transformations.

WITHOUT CDM (10 systems):
System A ←────────────→ System B  (unique transform A↔B)
System A ←────────────→ System C  (unique transform A↔C)
... (45 total bilateral transforms)

WITH CDM (10 systems):
System A → Canonical ← System B
System C → Canonical ← System D
... (10 transforms: one per system to/from CDM)

CDM in TOGAF:

  • Produced in Phase C Data Architecture
  • Stored as a Logical Data Diagram in the Architecture Definition Document (ADD)
  • Enables the integration patterns designed in Application Architecture (Phase C Part 2)
  • The CDM does NOT tell systems what their internal format must be — only what the shared exchange format is

CDM vs. Master Data Management — the distinction:

  • CDM = a FORMAT standard (how data is structured for exchange)
  • MDM = an AUTHORITY standard (which system holds the single authoritative record)
  • These are complementary: you use the CDM to exchange the authoritative MDM record

Master Data Management (MDM) — Four Styles

Master Data is the core shared data that multiple business processes depend on — Customer, Product, Supplier, Employee, Location. Inconsistent master data is one of the most common enterprise architecture problems.

MDM Implementation Styles:

Style 1: Registry Style

  • Each operational system retains its own master data copy
  • A central Registry stores cross-references (IDs) between systems — it does NOT store the actual data
  • When you need to find all records for "Customer XYZ," you query the Registry to find which system has what ID, then query each system
  • Best for: Organizations that cannot change operational systems; incremental adoption
  • Weakness: No single authoritative record; data quality still varies per system

Style 2: Consolidation Style

  • Data from all operational systems is periodically extracted and consolidated into a central MDM store
  • Operational systems continue to maintain their own records; the MDM store is for READ purposes (reporting, analytics)
  • Central store is NOT authoritative for operations — systems still update their own records
  • Best for: Reporting and analytics use cases; read-heavy; operational systems unchanged
  • Weakness: Central store can become stale between consolidation runs; not suitable for real-time operational decisions

Style 3: Coexistence Style

  • A central MDM store exists alongside operational systems
  • BOTH the MDM store AND the operational systems are authoritative — in their respective domains
  • Changes can originate in either the MDM store or operational systems; synchronization occurs bidirectionally
  • Best for: Large, complex environments where full centralization is not feasible; transition states during multi-year migrations
  • Weakness: Bidirectional synchronization is technically complex; conflict resolution requires governance

Style 4: Centralized Style

  • The central MDM store is the ONLY authoritative source of master data
  • All operational systems that need master data READ it from the central MDM store; they do NOT maintain their own copy
  • Any updates to master data happen ONLY in the MDM store
  • Best for: Maximum data quality control; organizations with strong governance maturity; greenfield implementations
  • Weakness: Highest implementation effort; requires operational systems to change; central store becomes a critical dependency
Exam tip

Know all four styles by name and their key characteristic. A scenario saying "multiple legacy systems cannot be modified, but a central cross-reference is needed" → Registry Style. "The organization needs a single authoritative record and all systems must use it" → Centralized Style. "Both the central store and operational systems will update records during a transition period" → Coexistence Style.

Data Lineage vs. Data Flow Diagrams — The Distinction

Both involve tracking data movement, but they serve fundamentally different purposes:

Data Lineage Data Flow Diagram (DFD)
Purpose Historical audit trail — where did this data COME FROM and what happened to it Architecture design — how does data CURRENTLY MOVE through the system
Direction Backward-looking (provenance) Current-state or target-state design
Use cases Regulatory compliance, root cause analysis, GDPR data subject requests Integration design, gap analysis, architecture documentation
Questions answered "This field in our report — where did it originate? What transformations changed it?" "How does customer data flow from the CRM to the analytics platform?"
TOGAF artifact type Data Lineage Diagram Data Flow Diagram
Primary driver Compliance, audit, data quality investigation Architecture design

Data Lineage is particularly relevant for:

  • Financial reporting (proving the source of numbers)
  • GDPR/privacy compliance (proving where personal data came from and where it went)
  • Data quality root cause analysis ("this field is wrong — where did the error enter?")

Data Sovereignty — Cross-Domain Impact

Data Sovereignty is the principle that data is subject to the laws of the country or jurisdiction in which it is collected or processed. This has become a major architectural constraint, particularly for organizations operating in regulated environments (financial services, healthcare, government) in jurisdictions like Saudi Arabia, the EU, or UAE.

Architectural implications of Data Sovereignty:

Domain How Data Sovereignty Affects It
Business Architecture Compliance processes; Data Governance accountability; legal obligations; organizational roles for compliance
Data Architecture Which data entities are subject to sovereignty requirements; data classification (sovereign vs non-sovereign); residency policies
Application Architecture Which applications process sovereign data; whether applications can be deployed in the required jurisdiction
Technology Architecture Where servers/data centers are located; cloud provider selection (must have data centers in required country); DR site location
Exam tip

Data sovereignty is a CROSS-CUTTING concern that affects ALL 4 architecture domains, not just Technology Architecture. This is a common exam trap — a scenario about data sovereignty requirements that asks "which architecture domains are affected?" — the answer is ALL FOUR.

Data Architecture Artifacts — Full Classification

Catalogs

Catalog What It Lists
Data Entity/Data Component Catalog All data entities, their attributes, and which systems own them
Business Service/Information Catalog Business services and the information they consume and produce
Data Governance Roles Catalog Data Owners, Data Stewards, and their responsibilities per data domain

Matrices

Matrix What It Shows Why It Matters
Data Entity/Business Function Matrix Which data entities are created, read, updated, deleted (CRUD) by which business functions Identifies data ownership, access patterns, redundancy
Data Entity/Application Matrix Which applications own which data entities (C) and which merely use them (RUD) Application rationalization decisions in Phase C Part 2
Data Quality Requirements Matrix Data entities × quality dimensions × required thresholds Governs data quality investment priorities

Diagrams

Diagram What It Shows
Conceptual Data Diagram High-level entities and their relationships (no attributes shown)
Logical Data Diagram / Entity-Relationship Diagram Full entities, attributes, and relationships (technology-independent)
Data Flow Diagram How data moves between processes, data stores, and external entities
Data Lineage Diagram Historical provenance trail of data from source through all transformations
Data Migration Diagram How data will be moved from old systems to new systems during migration
Data Security Diagram Data classification zones, access control boundaries, and security controls
Data Lifecycle Diagram How data is created, maintained, archived, and eventually destroyed
Exam tip

The Data Entity/Business Function Matrix uses CRUD notation (Create, Read, Update, Delete). A data entity is "Owned" by the function that Creates it. This matrix is used to identify which application or function has authority (ownership) over each data entity — a direct input to MDM design.

Key Takeaway for Day 2 (Data Architecture)

Data Architecture (Phase C Part 1) operates at three levels: Conceptual (entities only), Logical (entities + attributes, tech-independent), Physical (begins in Phase D). Six data quality dimensions: Accuracy, Completeness, Consistency, Timeliness, Validity, Uniqueness — know each by plain-language description, not just name. CDM solves format incompatibility (reduces N² transforms to N); MDM solves authority incompatibility (four styles: Registry, Consolidation, Coexistence, Centralized). Data Lineage = backward-looking audit trail; DFD = current-state architecture design. Data Sovereignty affects ALL 4 domains. The Data Entity/Business Function Matrix uses CRUD to identify data ownership.

Day 3 (Wednesday): Application Architecture — Applied Domain Deep Dive

Where Application Architecture Sits in the ADM

Application Architecture is the second sub-phase of Phase C. It is always done AFTER Data Architecture because applications must be designed to handle the data entities already defined — not the reverse.

The formal purpose: describe how the logical application components of the Target Architecture will be structured, the interfaces between them, and how they support the business functions and data requirements established in Phases B and C Part 1.

Phase C Application Architecture answers:

  • What applications exist in the organization, and what is their purpose? (Application Portfolio)
  • Which applications will be kept, replaced, or retired? (Portfolio Rationalization)
  • How do applications interact? (Integration architecture)
  • What is each application's technology fitness? (TIME model assessment)

Application Portfolio Rationalization — The TIME Model

The TIME Model is the standard framework for classifying every application in the portfolio based on two dimensions: Business Value (strategic importance) and Technical Health (quality of the technology).

Category Business Value Technical Health Decision Action
T — Tolerate Low Adequate Keep running; no investment Monitor; plan retirement when opportunity arises
I — Invest High Good Actively invest Add features; expand; grow
M — Migrate High Poor Preserve the function; replace the technology Re-platform to modern technology
E — Eliminate Low Any Remove from portfolio Decommission; plan the exit 
                    HIGH TECHNICAL HEALTH
                           │
         INVEST            │          MIGRATE
    (High value,           │      (High value,
     good technology)      │       poor technology)
                           │
HIGH ──────────────────────┼────────────────────── LOW
VALUE                      │                    VALUE
                           │
        TOLERATE           │          ELIMINATE
    (Low value,            │      (Low value,
     adequate technology)  │       any technology)
                           │
                    LOW TECHNICAL HEALTH

Applying the TIME Model in Phase C:

For each application in the portfolio, the architect asks:

  1. How important is this application's function to the business strategy? → Business Value rating
  2. How healthy is the technology? (Support status, vendor roadmap, integration capability, performance, security posture) → Technical Health rating
  3. Which TIME quadrant does this place the application in?
  4. What is the recommended action?

Detailed action guidance per category:

Tolerate:

  • The application does something necessary but not strategically differentiating
  • Technology is adequate (not great, but not broken)
  • Do NOT invest in new features or platform improvements
  • Monitor technical health — when it drops below "adequate," reassess
  • The key decision point: when vendor support expires → likely moves to Migrate or Eliminate
  • Example: A legacy payroll system that works, has vendor support until 2027, but payroll is not a strategic differentiator

Invest:

  • The application supports a strategic capability AND runs on good technology
  • Actively invest: new features, scalability improvements, user experience enhancements
  • Protect and grow this application
  • Example: A mobile banking app that is central to customer experience and runs on modern cloud-native technology

Migrate:

  • The application supports important business functions BUT the technology is poor (EOL platform, legacy infrastructure, no vendor support, security vulnerabilities)
  • The function is worth keeping; the technology is not
  • Solution: Re-platform the same function onto modern technology
  • This is the most complex TIME category — it requires a migration project
  • Example: An HR management system with critical employee data running on a 1990s mainframe with vendor support ending

Eliminate:

  • The application's function has low business value (either redundant with another system, replaceable manually, or no longer needed)
  • Technology health is irrelevant — even if it runs well, the function isn't worth the cost of maintaining it
  • Solution: Plan a decommission project; ensure any needed data is migrated
  • Example: A standalone expense reporting tool after the ERP already handles expenses
Exam tip

TIME model scenario questions give you a description and ask for the classification. The critical path: HIGH value + GOOD tech = Invest. HIGH value + POOR tech = Migrate. LOW value + any tech = Tolerate (if working) or Eliminate (if the function is no longer needed). The most common confusion is between Tolerate and Eliminate — Tolerate has adequate tech and the function is still needed (just not strategic); Eliminate is when the function should stop.

Integration Architecture — Five Core Patterns

Choosing the right integration pattern is one of the most scenario-tested Application Architecture decisions. You must know all five patterns: when to use each, its strengths, and its weaknesses.

Pattern 1: Point-to-Point

System A ◄──────────────────► System B
System A ◄──────────────────► System C
System B ◄──────────────────► System C
  • Each system connects directly to every other system it needs to communicate with
  • For N systems: N × (N−1) / 2 integration connections
  • Strength: Simple for a very small number of systems; each integration is independent
  • Weakness: Scales catastrophically — 10 systems = 45 connections; 20 systems = 190 connections; change in one system requires updating all its integrations
  • When to use: 2 to 4 systems maximum; stable, infrequent interfaces
  • When to avoid: More than 4 systems; when systems change frequently

Pattern 2: Hub-and-Spoke / Enterprise Service Bus (ESB)

System A ──────► ESB/HUB ◄────── System B
System C ──────►    │    ◄────── System D
                    │
              (Routes, transforms,
               and monitors messages)
  • All systems connect to a central hub; the hub routes and transforms messages between systems
  • For N systems: N connections (one per system to the hub)
  • Strength: Dramatically reduces connection complexity; central point for monitoring, logging, and governance; transformation logic centralized
  • Weakness: Hub is a single point of failure and a potential performance bottleneck; the hub itself becomes a complex, critical system to manage
  • When to use: Medium-to-large enterprises with many systems; when central governance of integration is needed; complex transformation requirements
  • When to avoid: Extremely high-throughput real-time requirements (hub adds latency)

Pattern 3: API Gateway

External Consumer ──► API Gateway ──► Service A
                           │──────────► Service B
                           └──────────► Service C
  • A single, managed entry point for EXTERNAL consumers accessing internal services
  • The Gateway handles: authentication, authorization, rate limiting, SSL termination, request routing, versioning, analytics
  • Strength: Single security enforcement point for external access; decouples external consumers from internal topology; enables versioning and analytics
  • Weakness: Adds latency; another system to manage; can become a bottleneck for external traffic
  • When to use: External-facing APIs; microservices environments; when external partners need to access multiple internal services through a single interface
  • When to avoid: Pure internal system-to-system integration (ESB is more appropriate for internal)

Pattern 4: Event-Driven Architecture / Message Broker (Publish-Subscribe)

Producer A ──► Message Broker ◄── Producer B
               ↓           ↓
         Consumer 1    Consumer 2
         (subscribed   (subscribed
          to Topic X)   to Topic X)
  • Producers publish events to a Message Broker without knowing who will consume them
  • Consumers subscribe to topics/queues and receive events independently
  • Fully asynchronous and decoupled — producers and consumers have no direct knowledge of each other
  • Strength: Complete decoupling (adding a new consumer requires no change to the producer); highly scalable; resilient (consumers process events when they are ready); natural fit for audit trails and event replay
  • Weakness: Harder to trace failures (asynchronous); eventual consistency (not immediate); complex debugging; requires careful topic/queue design
  • When to use: High-volume event streaming; when one event must notify multiple downstream systems simultaneously; when decoupling producers from consumers is critical; audit logs; IoT data ingestion
  • Examples: Apache Kafka, Azure Service Bus, AWS EventBridge, RabbitMQ

Pattern 5: Microservices Architecture

         API Gateway
              │
 ┌────────────┼────────────┐
 │            │            │
Order       Inventory   Payment
Service      Service     Service
 (owns       (owns       (owns
 order       stock       payment
  data)       data)       data)
  • An application is decomposed into small, independently deployable services
  • Each service owns its own data store; services communicate via APIs or events
  • Strength: Independent deployment and scaling per service; fault isolation (one service failing doesn't bring down the whole system); technology choice freedom per service; supports multiple autonomous development teams
  • Weakness: Distributed system complexity; network latency between services; data consistency across services requires careful design; significant operational overhead (many services to monitor and deploy)
  • When to use: Large applications where different capabilities have very different scaling needs; multiple autonomous teams building and deploying independently; when the organization has the DevOps maturity to manage many services
  • When to avoid: Small applications; teams new to distributed systems; when transactional consistency is paramount across many operations
Exam tip

Scenario questions for integration patterns work by elimination. Identify: Is this internal or external? (External → API Gateway). Is this one-to-many async notification? (→ Event-Driven). Is this "too many connections to manage"? (→ ESB/Hub-and-Spoke). Is this a large app with independent teams? (→ Microservices). Is this 2–3 systems that rarely change? (→ Point-to-Point is acceptable).

Day 4 (Thursday): Technology Architecture — Applied Domain Deep Dive

Where Technology Architecture Sits in the ADM

Technology Architecture is produced in Phase D. It is always done LAST among the four domains because it exists purely to SERVE the applications and data — technology decisions are meaningless without knowing what applications need to run and what data needs to be stored.

The formal purpose: describe the logical software and hardware capabilities required to support the deployment of business, data, and application services. This includes IT infrastructure, middleware, networks, communications, processing, and standards.

Phase D Technology Architecture answers:

  • What technology platforms and infrastructure are needed to run the target applications?
  • What cloud model best suits each application's requirements?
  • What are the reliability, availability, and performance requirements, and how do we meet them?
  • What technology standards govern the organization's IT landscape?
  • What is the lifecycle status of all current technology components?

Cloud Architecture — Service Models and Deployment Models

Cloud architecture decisions are a central Phase D concern. The exam tests both the service models (what the customer manages) and the deployment models (where the infrastructure is).

Cloud Service Models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS)

The key differentiator: what does the CUSTOMER manage vs. what does the PROVIDER manage?

                     CUSTOMER MANAGES:
SaaS ────────── Configuration and data only
(Software as    Everything else managed by provider
 a Service)     Examples: Microsoft 365, Salesforce, SAP S/4HANA Cloud

PaaS ────────── Application code + data
(Platform as    OS, runtime, infrastructure managed by provider
 a Service)     Examples: Azure App Service, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Google App Engine

IaaS ────────── OS + middleware + application + data
(Infrastructure Virtual machines, storage, networking provided by vendor

Choosing between service models (exam scenario approach):

  • "Organization wants cloud but needs to control the operating system" → IaaS
  • "Organization wants to deploy a custom application without managing servers" → PaaS
  • "Organization wants to use a fully managed email and collaboration platform" → SaaS
  • "Organization has strict compliance requirements and cannot put data in any shared cloud" → On-Premise or Private Cloud

Cloud Deployment Models

Model Who Owns/Operates Infrastructure Key Characteristic Best For
Private Cloud Single organization (on-premises or hosted exclusively) Maximum control, security, compliance; highest cost Financial services, healthcare, government; regulated data; strict compliance
Public Cloud Cloud provider; shared among many customers Lowest cost; elastic scaling; least control Non-sensitive workloads; variable demand; innovation; start-up speed

High Availability and Disaster Recovery Patterns

These are core Phase D design decisions, driven by business continuity requirements that originate in Business Architecture.

High Availability (HA) — Protecting Against Component Failure

Active-Active:

         Load Balancer
         /           \
   Server A        Server B
  (ACTIVE)        (ACTIVE)
  Both handling traffic simultaneously
  • Both (or all) servers handle production traffic simultaneously
  • Load balancer distributes requests across all active servers
  • If one server fails, the load balancer routes all traffic to remaining servers — no user impact
  • RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Near-zero (seconds)
  • Cost: Higher — all servers are always running
  • When to use: Mission-critical systems; high-traffic applications; when any downtime is unacceptable

Active-Passive (Active-Standby):

         Load Balancer
         /           \
   Server A        Server B
  (ACTIVE)        (PASSIVE/STANDBY)
  Handling all traffic   Monitoring; activates if A fails
  • Primary server handles all traffic; standby server monitors but does not serve requests
  • On primary failure, failover occurs — brief downtime during switchover (seconds to minutes)
  • RTO: Minutes (depends on switchover speed)
  • Cost: Lower — standby server not handling production load (though it must be running)
  • When to use: Systems where brief downtime is acceptable; cost-sensitive environments; less critical systems

Disaster Recovery (DR) — Protecting Against Site-Level Failure

DR goes beyond HA (which handles server failures) to handle complete facility or regional failures.

DR Approach Description RTO RPO Cost
Hot Standby Full replica running and synchronized in real-time at DR site Minutes Near-zero (seconds) Highest
Warm Standby Reduced-scale replica running; scales up to full capacity on failover Hours Minutes to hours Medium
Cold Standby Infrastructure exists at DR site but is not running; must be started and restored Days Hours to days Low
Backup & Restore No standby infrastructure; restore from backups to new infrastructure Days to weeks Hours to days Lowest

RPO (Recovery Point Objective): Maximum acceptable data loss — how recent must the last good backup be?
RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Maximum acceptable downtime — how long can the system be unavailable?

Exam tip

Active-Active = both sides serving simultaneously (no failover needed, just load redistribution). Active-Passive = one active, one waiting (brief failover downtime). Hot/Warm/Cold Standby = DR options at the site level. The choice is always driven by the business's RTO/RPO requirements, which come from Business Architecture (business continuity requirements).

Technology Standards — Four Categories

The Phase D deliverable includes a Technology Standards Catalog that classifies every technology in use or under consideration. There are exactly four categories:

Category Meaning Implication Example
Mandatory Must be used; no exceptions without Architecture Board approval All projects must use this technology "All APIs must use HTTPS/TLS 1.3 or higher"
Recommended Should be used; alternatives require justification to Architecture Board Default choice; deviation needs a reason "Recommended RDBMS is PostgreSQL 16"
Emerging New technology approved for limited/experimental use; under evaluation Can be used on new projects with approval; not yet proven at scale "GraphQL is approved for new API projects; evaluation period 12 months"
Retiring Being phased out; no new projects may use it; existing uses must migrate No new adoption; create migration plan "Oracle 11g — no new projects; existing systems must migrate by end of 2027"

Why technology standards matter for the exam:

  • The Technology Standards Catalog is a key Phase D output stored in the Standards Information Base (Layer 4 of the Architecture Repository)
  • Standards prevent "technology zoo" proliferation — different teams choosing incompatible technologies
  • Standards violations discovered in Phase G (Compliance Assessment) create Non-conformant findings
  • Standards in "Retiring" category drive Phase H Technology Triggers
Exam tip

Know all four categories. A scenario saying "a technology approved for experimental use on pilot projects while the Architecture Board evaluates it" → Emerging (not Recommended, not Provisional — the TOGAF term is Emerging). A scenario saying "the organization has decided this technology must not be used for any new work but existing systems don't need to change immediately" → Retiring.

Day 5 (Friday): Cross-Domain Cascade Analysis, Trade-offs, and Architecture Decisions

The Cascade Principle — Formal Definition

The Cascade Principle states that changes in Business Architecture drive changes in Data and Application Architecture, which in turn drive changes in Technology Architecture. The direction of influence is always top-down: Business → Information Systems (Data + Application) → Technology.

This is not just a design guideline — it is built into the ADM sequence:

Phase B: Business Architecture
           |
           | (Business needs drive data and application requirements)
           v
Phase C: Information Systems Architecture
  Part 1: Data Architecture      (What data entities, quality, flows)
  Part 2: Application Architecture   (What applications, integrations)
           |
           | (Application and data requirements drive technology choices)
           v
Phase D: Technology Architecture
           (Infrastructure, cloud, standards to support apps and data)

The reverse is never true. Technology decisions are always downstream of business decisions.

Extended Cascade Example — Saudi Bank Adding Open Banking

Trigger: SAMA issues a regulation requiring the bank to expose customer account data and payment initiation to licensed third-party providers via standardized APIs.

Phase B — Business Architecture Changes:

  • New Business Capability: "Open Banking API Provision" (must be created)
  • New Business Process: Third-party application onboarding and consent management
  • New Regulatory Obligation: SAMA Open Banking Framework compliance
  • New Roles: Open Banking Product Owner, Regulatory Compliance Officer
  • New Objective: "Onboard 10 licensed third-party providers within 6 months of go-live"

Phase C Part 1 — Data Architecture Changes (driven by Phase B):

  • New Data Entities: Third-Party Provider (TPP), Consent Record, API Access Token, Transaction Log
  • New Data Quality Requirements: Consent Records must be immutable (Validity dimension); Transaction Logs must be complete (Completeness dimension)
  • New Data Sovereignty Constraint: Customer financial data shared via APIs must remain in KSA data centers
  • Gap: No Consent Record entity exists in current architecture

Phase C Part 2 — Application Architecture Changes (driven by Phase B + Data):

  • New Application: Open Banking API Gateway (TIME = Invest — new, strategic)
  • New Application: Developer Portal for third-party onboarding (TIME = Invest)
  • Existing Core Banking System: add Open Banking API interface
  • Integration Pattern Change: API Gateway pattern added for external access
  • New Service Contracts for all Open Banking API endpoints
  • Gap: No Developer Portal exists — must be acquired or built

Phase D — Technology Architecture Changes (driven by Data + Application):

  • New infrastructure: API Gateway platform (cloud PaaS)
  • Developer Portal hosting (cloud PaaS)
  • Enhanced security: mTLS, OAuth 2.0 + PKCE, rate limiting, DDoS protection
  • Cloud Deployment Constraint: KSA-region required for data sovereignty
  • New Mandatory Standard: OAuth 2.0 + PKCE for all Open Banking API authentication
  • Gap: Current cloud deployment is in Europe — must add KSA region

This single regulatory change cascades into all four domains. Exam scenario questions will describe a situation like this and ask which phase produces a specific artifact, or which domain is responsible for a specific constraint.

Cross-Domain Consistency Rules

After all four domains are designed, these rules must hold in the Target Architecture. Any violation is an architecture gap generating a Work Package in Phase E.

Rule Statement Violation =
Rule 1 Every application must have a technology home Technology Architecture is incomplete
Rule 2 Every data entity must have an application that creates it (C in CRUD) Data entity will never be populated
Rule 3 Every business capability must be supported by at least one application Capability cannot be exercised
Rule 4 Technology choices must enable all application requirements (availability, performance) Application SLAs cannot be met
Rule 5 Data entities must correspond to business entities defined in Business Architecture Orphaned data with no business meaning

Architecture Trade-offs — Formal Approach

Architecture trade-offs are situations where all stakeholder requirements cannot be simultaneously satisfied. TOGAF requires architects to identify, document, escalate (to Architecture Board when significant), and formally record trade-off resolutions in ADRs.

The Seven Common Architecture Trade-offs:

Trade-off Tension Key Resolution Factors
Security vs. Performance Encryption and authentication add latency Regulatory requirements; data classification; user tolerance
Standardization vs. Flexibility Rigid standards reduce agility; flexible choices increase complexity Rate of change; team size; governance maturity
Centralization vs. Distribution Central control reduces duplication; distribution improves resilience Network reliability; organizational autonomy; trust levels
Cost vs. Reliability Redundancy and HA increase cost Business criticality; cost of downtime vs. cost of redundancy
Tight Integration vs. Loose Coupling Tight = efficient; loose = resilient and scalable Rate of change; future scalability; team autonomy
Buy vs. Build COTS is faster but constrained; custom is flexible but expensive Competitive differentiation; budget; time-to-market
Short-term vs. Long-term Tactical wins vs. sustainable architecture Business pressure; technical debt; strategic horizon

How TOGAF handles trade-offs:

  1. Architecture Principles (from Preliminary Phase) pre-resolve common trade-offs before they arise
  2. ADRs formally capture each significant trade-off resolution with rationale
  3. Architecture Board escalation for trade-offs affecting multiple projects or large investments
  4. Rationale section of ADD documents why design decisions were made

Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) — Full Coverage

An ADR captures a significant architecture decision, its context, and consequences. ADRs create institutional memory of WHY the architecture looks the way it does — preventing future teams from re-opening settled decisions without understanding the original reasoning.

Six ADR Components:

Component Description Example
Title Short unique identifier "ADR-047: Event-Driven Integration for Order Processing"
Status Current state of the decision Proposed → Accepted → Deprecated → Superseded
Context The problem requiring a decision; constraints in place "30 systems need to exchange order events. Current P2P has 435 connections."
Decision The choice made — unambiguous "Implement Apache Kafka; all order events published as Kafka topics"
Rationale WHY this choice; rejected alternatives and why "Kafka preferred over RabbitMQ for throughput and event replay. ESB rejected for latency at scale."
Consequences Positive AND negative outcomes "(+) Decoupled, scalable, replayable. (-) Eventual consistency; requires Kafka expertise."

Where ADRs live: Governance Log — Layer 6 of the Architecture Repository (the permanent audit trail).

ADR Status lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted → Deprecated → Superseded

Exam tip

When a question asks "how does TOGAF ensure architecture decisions are documented with rationale for future reference?" → ADRs in the Governance Log. When a scenario describes "a document capturing a technology choice, the alternatives rejected, and both positive and negative consequences" → that is an ADR.

Architecture Debt Across All Four Domains

Architecture Debt is the accumulated deviation from the approved architecture. It grows through: dispensations never remediated, deferred migrations, emergency workarounds that became permanent, and implementation changes never reviewed by the Architecture Board.

Domain-specific debt patterns:

Business Architecture Debt: Processes redesigned in Target Architecture but never implemented; roles defined but never staffed; governance documented but not enforced.

Data Architecture Debt: MDM consolidation planned but deferred; data quality standards in ARS not enforced; new data flows created without updating the Data Lineage Diagram.

Application Architecture Debt: Eliminate-classified applications still running; P2P integrations supposed to migrate to ESB but not migrated; service contracts defined but ignored.

Technology Architecture Debt: EOL systems with unpatched security vulnerabilities; Retiring standards with systems that haven't migrated; temporary workarounds that became permanent.

Managing Architecture Debt (Phase H):

  1. Maintain a debt register with each item, its risk, and remediation cost estimate
  2. Prioritize by risk — security-risk debt (EOL, known vulnerabilities) first
  3. Include debt remediation as Work Packages in the Architecture Roadmap
  4. All Dispensations granted in Phase G must include a remediation deadline — those without deadlines become permanent debt

Key Takeaway for Day 5 (Cross-Domain)

The Cascade Principle is non-negotiable: Business drives Data and Application, which drive Technology — always in this direction. Cross-domain consistency rules provide a systematic checklist for Gap Analysis: every application needs a technology home; every data entity needs an application owner; every capability needs application support; technology must enable application requirements; data must correspond to business entities. Architecture Trade-offs are inevitable and must be formally captured in ADRs (6 components: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Rationale, Consequences) stored in the Governance Log. Architecture Debt accumulates in all four domains and is managed in Phase H through a debt register, risk prioritization, and roadmap remediation.

Day 6 (Saturday): TOGAF Integration with Other Frameworks

Why This Matters for the Exam

TOGAF does not exist in isolation. Real organizations use TOGAF alongside ITIL, COBIT, project management frameworks, Agile methods, and data management standards. The exam tests whether you understand how TOGAF connects with these complementary frameworks — specifically which TOGAF activities align with which framework activities, and what each framework contributes that TOGAF does not.

The integration questions are not hard if you understand the principle: TOGAF designs and governs; complementary frameworks manage and operate. Each integration follows the same basic logic: TOGAF defines WHAT the architecture should be; the complementary framework defines HOW the operational activity is carried out.

TOGAF and ITIL

ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library): A globally adopted framework for IT Service Management (ITSM) — the practices for managing and operating IT services in production.

The fundamental relationship: TOGAF designs and blueprints the IT environment. ITIL manages and operates it.

TOGAF (Design Phase)          ITIL (Operations)
Phase A-F: Design and plan    Service Transition: Build and deploy
Phase G: Govern implementation Change Management: Control changes to production
Phase H: Monitor for changes  Service Operation: Run production services
                              Problem Management: Fix recurring failures

Key TOGAF-ITIL integration points:

TOGAF Activity ITIL Process How They Connect
Architecture Contracts (Phase F) define compliance requirements Change Management (Change Advisory Board) Architecture Contracts define WHAT must be built; ITIL Change Records control HOW changes enter production. The Architecture Board and Change Advisory Board must coordinate.
Phase G: Compliance Assessment of implementation Change Management CAB approval Before a project goes live (Phase G), ITIL Change Management must approve the change to production. The Compliance Assessment (TOGAF) and Change Record (ITIL) are complementary — one checks architecture compliance, the other controls production risk.
Phase H: Monitoring deployed architecture for change triggers Event Management ITIL Event Management monitors IT systems and raises alerts. Events that indicate architecture-level issues become input to Phase H monitoring.
Phase H: Responding to operational problems that indicate architectural issues Problem Management ITIL Problem Management identifies root causes of recurring incidents. When a root cause is architectural (e.g., a fundamentally wrong integration design), it becomes a Phase H Architecture Change Request.
Phase G/H: Ensuring deployed systems meet SLAs defined in ARS Service Level Management The performance requirements in the Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS) become the basis for SLAs managed by ITIL Service Level Management.

Key Integration Principle: When TOGAF architecture changes need to go into production, they MUST go through ITIL Change Management. The Architecture Contract (TOGAF) defines WHAT must be built to what standard; the ITIL Change Record documents HOW and WHEN it will be deployed to production. These two documents work together.

Exam tip

"TOGAF designs; ITIL manages." The most commonly tested connection: Phase G Implementation Governance ↔ ITIL Change Management. Phase H Architecture Change Management ↔ ITIL Problem Management (when operational problems reveal architectural root causes). A scenario saying "changes to the production system must be approved by an IT operations committee before deployment" → ITIL Change Management operating alongside TOGAF Phase G.

COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies): A framework for IT Governance and Management — ensuring IT is aligned with business strategy, properly controlled, and subject to audit.

The fundamental relationship: TOGAF provides architectural direction and methodology. COBIT provides governance controls and audit mechanisms.

TOGAF                         COBIT

Architecture Board decisions  Governance bodies (Board, Executive Committee)
Compliance Assessments        Control objectives and audit processes
Architecture Principles       Policies and principles
Dispensations (waivers)       Risk acceptance processes

TOGAF Element Related COBIT Element Relationship

Architecture Governance Framework COBIT governance framework TOGAF's Architecture Governance can be implemented using COBIT's governance structure
Compliance Assessments (Phase G) COBIT control objectives and audit processes Architecture Compliance Assessments can be aligned with COBIT audits to reduce duplication
Architecture Principles COBIT policies and principles Architecture Principles can be derived from or aligned with COBIT policy statements
Architecture Repository COBIT configuration management Architecture Repository artifacts complement COBIT's CMDB (Configuration Management Database)

TOGAF is an architecture development method; COBIT is a governance and audit framework. They are complementary, not competing. A scenario asking "the organization wants to use TOGAF for architecture development AND ensure strong IT governance controls and auditability" → use TOGAF and COBIT together.

TOGAF and Project Management Frameworks (PRINCE2, PMI PMBOK)

PRINCE2 / PMI PMBOK: Structured project management frameworks for planning, executing, monitoring, and closing projects.

The fundamental relationship: TOGAF produces the architecture blueprint (what to build). Project management delivers it (how to build it, on time and budget).

Key TOGAF-Project Management integration points:

TOGAF Output Project Management Input Relationship
Statement of Architecture Work (Phase A) Project Brief / Project Mandate The SOW defines the scope and constraints of the architecture project; this feeds the project's initiation documents
Architecture Contracts (Phase F) Project Contract / Statement of Work The Architecture Contract defines WHAT must be built and to what quality standards; the project contract governs HOW and WHEN
Work Packages (Phase E) Projects / Workstreams in Programme Management Each Work Package becomes one or more projects in the implementation programme

Key Integration Principle: The Architecture Contract (TOGAF Phase F output) feeds into the project initiation documents — either the PRINCE2 Project Initiation Document (PID) or the PMBOK Project Charter. Architecture governance and project governance must have defined escalation paths between them: the Architecture Board and Project Board must know how to resolve conflicts.

Exam tip

A scenario saying "the architecture team produced a document specifying what must be built, quality standards, and acceptance criteria; this document was then used as the basis for the project's contract with the development team" → the TOGAF Architecture Contract feeding into the project's Statement of Work.

TOGAF and Agile / SAFe

Agile: An iterative, incremental approach to software delivery (Scrum, Kanban, etc.) SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework): A framework for scaling Agile to large enterprises with multiple teams.

The perceived tension: TOGAF requires upfront analysis and design (Phases A–F before any development); Agile prefers just-in-time design and emergent solutions. This appears to be a conflict.

The resolution: TOGAF provides the guardrails (the architecture) within which Agile teams operate (the delivery). They operate at different levels and timeframes.

TOGAF (Strategic/Architecture Level)     Agile (Delivery Level)
Phase A-F: Define architecture guardrails ─► Teams build within guardrails
Architecture Runway maintained by EA       Agile sprints consume the runway
Phase H: Monitor and extend runway ◄────── Teams signal when runway is insufficient

Architecture Runway (SAFe Concept)

The Architecture Runway is the existing code, components, and technical infrastructure sufficient to support near-term Agile development without requiring significant architectural work first. The Enterprise Architecture team maintains the runway by designing architectural decisions ahead of development teams — so teams always have a solid foundation to build on.

How it works:

  • EA team (using TOGAF ADM) works 1–2 Program Increments ahead of development teams
  • When development teams complete a feature, they consume some of the architecture runway
  • EA must continuously extend the runway before teams reach its end
  • If teams reach the end of the runway before EA extends it, they face an "architectural blocker" — they cannot proceed without architectural decisions that haven't been made yet

In TOGAF terms:

  • The Architecture Roadmap (Phase E/F output) defines the runway
  • Phase H monitors the runway — watching for development teams approaching its edge
  • A new abbreviated ADM cycle (or loop to Phase E) is triggered when the runway needs extending

Applying ADM in Agile Contexts

TOGAF Part III explicitly supports using ADM in Agile contexts through:

  1. Abbreviated ADM cycles: Run lightweight, rapid ADM iterations aligned to Program Increments (PI) or release cycles rather than running the full 9-phase cycle for every change
  2. Just-Enough Architecture: Design only what is needed for the near term; elaborate as understanding grows. Avoid over-engineering architecture for features that may not be built
  3. Architecture as Constraints (not Commands): EA defines boundaries, principles, and non-negotiables; development teams have freedom of choice within those boundaries
  4. Segment Architecture: Focus detailed ADM work on specific segments (domains, business units, capabilities) rather than trying to define enterprise-wide architecture all at once
Exam tip

TOGAF and Agile are NOT opposed — they operate at different levels. TOGAF is the strategic architectural framework; Agile is the delivery method. The Architecture Runway (SAFe) is the key concept reconciling them. A scenario asking "how can a SAFe organization use TOGAF without slowing down Agile teams?" → EA maintains an Architecture Runway using abbreviated ADM cycles; teams work within architectural guardrails without waiting for full ADM completion.

TOGAF and the Zachman Framework

Zachman Framework: An enterprise architecture classification framework (ontology) organized as a 6×6 matrix:

  • Columns (Interrogatives — the Questions): What, How, Where, Who, When, Why
  • Rows (Perspectives — the Audience): Executive (Planner), Business Management (Owner), Architect (Designer), Engineer (Builder), Technician (Subcontractor), User

The fundamental distinction:

TOGAF Zachman Framework
Type Process framework — a METHOD for developing enterprise architecture Classification framework — an ONTOLOGY for categorizing architecture artifacts
Core element ADM (a step-by-step process) 6x6 matrix (a taxonomy)
Provides Steps, phases, governance, techniques for doing EA A vocabulary and classification system for what EA produces
Does NOT provide A taxonomy for every artifact type A process for developing architecture
Used for Guiding HOW to develop architecture Classifying and organizing architecture artifacts

Using TOGAF and Zachman Together:

  • Use TOGAF ADM to guide the PROCESS of developing architecture (what phases to follow, what to produce, how to govern)
  • Use the Zachman Framework to CLASSIFY and ORGANIZE the artifacts TOGAF's ADM produces

The TOGAF Content Framework (Part IV — covered in Week 4) serves some of the same classification purpose as Zachman — but they are not the same. Zachman is more comprehensive as a taxonomy; TOGAF Content Framework is specifically aligned with the ADM.

Exam tip

This is a direct, common exam question: "What is the fundamental difference between TOGAF and the Zachman Framework?" → TOGAF is a process (method for developing enterprise architecture); Zachman is a classification framework (ontology for categorizing and organizing architecture artifacts). They are complementary. Organizations can use TOGAF to develop architecture and Zachman to classify what they produce.

DAMA-DMBOK (Data Management Body of Knowledge): The industry standard for data management practices, organized into 11 Knowledge Areas including Data Governance, Data Quality, Master and Reference Data, Metadata Management, and more.

The fundamental relationship: TOGAF provides the data architecture (what data entities exist, how they relate, how data flows). DAMA-DMBOK provides the data management practices (how data is governed, quality-managed, stewarded, and maintained operationally).

Your CDMP Advantage: As a CDMP Associate candidate (85% score), you already understand DAMA-DMBOK deeply. This gives you a significant advantage in TOGAF's Data Architecture questions:

  • Data governance roles referenced in TOGAF (Data Owner, Data Steward, CDO) are DAMA concepts you know

TOGAF and DAMA-DMBOK are complementary frameworks at different levels. TOGAF defines data architecture; DAMA defines data management practice. They are NOT alternatives — organizations use both. A scenario asking "which framework should govern the day-to-day data quality management practices?" → DAMA-DMBOK. A scenario asking "which framework should be used to design the enterprise data model and data flows?" → TOGAF (specifically Phase C Data Architecture).
