Business Architecture Questions (Q1–Q8)

Q1. In the Business Motivation Model, which of the following BEST describes an Objective?

A) A broad qualitative desired result that supports the Vision
B) What the organization does — its fundamental activity
C) A SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound) target that supports a Goal
D) A broad approach for achieving a Goal

Answer: C — Objective = SMART, measurable, time-bound. A = Goal. B = Mission. D = Strategy.

Q2. An architect is creating a diagram that shows ALL the categories of activities that create value for an organization — from raw material acquisition through customer service — at a high strategic level. The categories shown are the same ones used by any company in the same industry. What is this diagram?

A) Value Stream Map
B) Business Capability Map
C) Value Chain Diagram
D) Functional Decomposition Diagram

Answer: C — Value Chain (Porter's model) = generic categories of ALL value-creating activities; applies to any organization in the same sector. Value Stream = specific end-to-end sequence for one outcome. Capability Map = strategic capabilities hierarchy. Functional Decomposition = hierarchical breakdown of functions.

Q3. (Scenario) A Business Architect is documenting the complete set of activities that must happen from the moment a customer submits a mortgage application to the moment the mortgage is approved and funds are disbursed. The diagram shows every step, every handoff between departments, every decision point, and the expected time at each step. What type of artifact is being created?

A) Value Chain Diagram
B) Value Stream Map
C) Business Capability Map
D) Process/Event/Control/Product Catalog

Answer: B — Value Stream Map: specific, end-to-end activity sequence for one specific outcome (mortgage approval and disbursement) for one specific stakeholder (mortgage applicant). Shows all steps, handoffs, and decision points — exactly a Value Stream.

Q4. (Scenario) A BPMN diagram for an invoice approval process shows two pools: one labeled "Supplier" and one labeled "Purchasing Department." An arrow connects the Supplier pool to the Purchasing Department pool when the supplier submits the invoice document. What type of arrow is this?

A) Sequence Flow
B) Association
C) Message Flow
D) Data Flow

Answer: C — Message Flow (dashed arrow): communication between two separate Pools (separate participants). Sequence Flow is within a single Pool. The Supplier and Purchasing Department are separate participants — communication between them is Message Flow.

Q5. Which statement BEST distinguishes a Business Capability from a Business Process?

A) Business Capabilities describe how work is done; Business Processes describe what the organization can do
B) Business Capabilities describe what the organization can do (stable, strategic); Business Processes describe how a specific activity is performed step-by-step (operational, changeable)
C) Business Capabilities are modeled in BPMN; Business Processes are modeled in Capability Maps
D) They are different names for the same concept at different organizational levels

Answer: B — Capability = WHAT (stable, strategic, expressed as a noun). Process = HOW (sequential, operational, expressed as a verb sequence). They operate at fundamentally different levels of abstraction. A is backwards. C is backwards (BPMN models Processes; Capability Maps show Capabilities).

Q6. (Scenario) A Business Architecture review reveals that three different departments (Sales, Finance, and Operations) each maintain their own "Customer" record, and each defines "Customer" differently. The Sales department says a Customer is "anyone who has inquired"; Finance says it is "anyone with an active contract"; Operations says it is "anyone who has received a delivery." The architecture team identifies this as a conflict to resolve in Phase C. What type of Phase C artifact will be used to define the single authoritative definition?

A) Application Interaction Matrix
B) Canonical Data Model
C) Data Flow Diagram
D) Business Service/Information Catalog

Answer: B — Canonical Data Model: a single enterprise-wide representation of a data entity (in this case, "Customer") that all systems agree to use for exchange. It resolves format and definition incompatibility. The CDM will establish the single authoritative Customer entity definition.

Q7. The Business Footprint Diagram is produced in Phase B. What unique information does it show that other Phase B diagrams do NOT?

A) The step-by-step process flows for all business activities
B) The organizational reporting hierarchy and headcount
C) The traceability from business drivers (Goals and Objectives) through organizational units and functions to the business services that fulfill them
D) The BPMN model of the most critical business process

Answer: C — The Business Footprint Diagram is the unique diagram that traces the "why architecture exists" chain: business Goals/Objectives → organizational units → business functions → business services. No other Phase B diagram shows this full traceability. A = BPMN Process Diagram. B = Organizational Map. D = BPMN diagram.

Q8. (Scenario) During a Phase B Gap Analysis, the architecture team identifies that the Target Business Architecture requires a "Digital Self-Service Onboarding" capability that does not exist in the current state. No application supports this capability, no process documents it, and no organizational unit owns it. How is this gap classified, and what happens to it next?

A) Technology Gap — escalated to Phase D
B) Data Gap — addressed in Phase C Part 1
C) Capability Gap in Business Architecture — becomes a Work Package candidate in Phase E
D) Process Gap — resolved by rewriting the BPMN process model

Answer: C — A capability that exists in the Target Architecture but not in the Baseline Architecture is a Capability Gap — the most strategic type of Business Architecture gap. All gaps from Phase B, C, and D feed into Phase E (Opportunities & Solutions) where they become Work Package candidates on the Architecture Roadmap. This gap will require new capability, process, application, and possibly technology Work Packages.

Data Architecture Questions (Q9–Q16)

Q9. (Scenario) An audit of the organization's CRM system finds that 28% of customer records have a blank phone number field, and 19% have no email address recorded. The data team also finds that 5% of records have the same customer entered twice under slightly different name spellings. Which TWO data quality dimensions are being violated?

A) Accuracy and Validity
B) Completeness and Uniqueness
C) Timeliness and Consistency
D) Consistency and Validity

Answer: B — Missing required fields (phone, email) = Completeness violation. Same customer appearing twice = Uniqueness violation. Accuracy would mean the data is present but wrong. Consistency would mean the same data looks different across systems. The question describes two distinct violations.

Q10. (Scenario) A financial services organization has 12 enterprise systems, each using a different format for "Account" data. Currently, every pair of systems that needs to exchange Account data requires a custom transformation — there are 66 transformations in total. The architecture team proposes establishing a single standardized Account data format that all systems use when exchanging account information. What solution is being proposed, and how many transformations will be needed after implementation?

A) Master Data Management (MDM); 12 transformations
B) Data Lineage tracking; 1 transformation
C) Canonical Data Model (CDM); 12 transformations
D) Data Quality Management; 6 transformations

Answer: C — CDM: a single exchange format reduces N×(N-1)/2 = 12×11/2 = 66 transformations to N = 12 transformations (one per system to/from the CDM). MDM addresses authority (which system is authoritative), not format. Data Lineage is backward-looking audit, not a format standard.

Q11. An organization is implementing MDM for its Supplier master data. After analysis, the architect recommends that existing supplier systems must not be changed, but a central cross-reference store should be created that maps supplier IDs across all systems so that a single supplier can be found regardless of which system originally created the record. The operational systems remain authoritative. Which MDM style is this?

A) Centralized Style
B) Coexistence Style
C) Consolidation Style
D) Registry Style

Answer: D — Registry Style: a central store holds only cross-references (ID mappings); all operational data stays in the original systems; original systems remain authoritative. No data is copied to the central store — only references. Centralized = central store is the ONLY authority. Coexistence = both central and operational are authoritative. Consolidation = a read-only central copy for reporting.

Q12. (Scenario) A compliance officer asks: "For this specific customer record in our data warehouse, can you tell me exactly where the data came from, what transformations it went through, and who modified it at each step?" The data architect says the required information exists in a specific type of diagram. What type is it?

A) Data Flow Diagram
B) Data Migration Diagram
C) Data Lineage Diagram
D) Logical Data Diagram

Answer: C — Data Lineage Diagram: shows the historical provenance of data — where it originated, all transformation steps, and movement history. This is the compliance and audit tool. A Data Flow Diagram shows current operational flows (architecture design), not historical provenance.

Q13. A data quality requirement states: "All trade orders must be captured in the system within 2 minutes of execution." Which data quality dimension does this requirement address?

A) Accuracy
B) Validity
C) Completeness
D) Timeliness

Answer: D — Timeliness: data is available when needed and is sufficiently current. The "within 2 minutes" specification is a timeliness requirement — it defines how quickly data must be captured and available. Accuracy would concern whether the trade details are correctly recorded.

Q14. (Scenario) A Saudi e-commerce company has received legal advice that all purchase history data for Saudi citizens must be stored and processed within the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The company currently uses a US-based cloud provider. The architecture team must now redesign the architecture to comply. Which architecture domains are affected?

A) Technology Architecture only — it is purely an infrastructure location question
B) Data Architecture and Technology Architecture only
C) Business Architecture and Technology Architecture only
D) All four architecture domains — Business, Data, Application, and Technology

Answer: D — Data sovereignty is a cross-cutting concern affecting ALL FOUR domains: Business (compliance processes, legal accountability, governance roles); Data (which entities are subject, data classification, residency policies); Application (which applications process affected data and whether they can run in KSA); Technology (where servers are, which cloud provider to use, where DR sites must be). "Technology only" is the common wrong answer.

Q15. What is the difference between a Conceptual Data Diagram and a Logical Data Diagram in Phase C?

A) They are the same artifact referred to by different names
B) A Conceptual Diagram shows high-level entities and relationships only (no attributes); a Logical Data Diagram shows entities, all attributes, and all relationships in a technology-independent, normalized form
C) A Conceptual Diagram is produced in Phase D; a Logical Diagram in Phase C
D) A Logical Diagram is for business stakeholders; a Conceptual Diagram is for technical teams

Answer: B — Conceptual = entities and relationships only (no attributes — simplest level, for business communication). Logical = full entities with attributes and relationships, technology-independent (for architecture design). Physical = specific database tables and data types (emerges in Phase D). B correctly distinguishes them. D has the audience backwards — Conceptual is actually more accessible to business stakeholders.

Q16. (Scenario) A TOGAF architect is working on Phase C Data Architecture and needs to determine which application is the authoritative "owner" of the Customer data entity — meaning which application is the only one that should be able to create new Customer records. Which Phase C artifact most directly shows this information?

A) Data Flow Diagram
B) Data Entity/Business Function Matrix
C) Data Lineage Diagram
D) Logical Data Diagram

Answer: B — The Data Entity/Business Function Matrix shows CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) relationships between data entities and business functions. The function (and therefore application supporting it) that has "C" (Create) for the Customer entity is the Owner. No other artifact directly shows data ownership in this way.

Application Architecture Questions (Q17–Q24)

Q17. (Scenario) An Application Architecture review classifies a Supply Chain Management system as follows: it supports a highly strategic business capability (supply chain execution is a key competitive differentiator), but it runs on a platform that is 18 years old, has no vendor support remaining, cannot integrate with modern APIs, and has serious security vulnerabilities. What TIME classification applies and what action is recommended?

A) Tolerate — the system still runs; keep it as-is
B) Eliminate — the old technology makes it worthless
C) Migrate — high business value, poor technical health; preserve the function, replace the technology
D) Invest — it is strategic, so invest in improving it

Answer: C — Migrate: High business value (strategic SCM capability) + Poor technical health (18-year-old platform, no support, security vulnerabilities) = Migrate. The function must be preserved (it is strategic); the technology must be replaced. Invest requires GOOD technology. Eliminate requires LOW value. Tolerate requires LOW value AND adequate technology.

Q18. An organization with 15 enterprise systems currently has 105 point-to-point interfaces. They implement an Enterprise Service Bus. After migration, how many interfaces will there be, and what is the mathematical principle?

A) 105 interfaces — ESB just centralizes the existing ones
B) 15 interfaces — one per system to the hub; N interfaces for N systems
C) 30 interfaces — bidirectional connections, one in and one out per system
D) 7 interfaces — roughly half, since duplicates are eliminated

Answer: B — ESB reduces from N×(N-1)/2 to N. For 15 systems: 15×14/2 = 105 P2P; with ESB = 15 (one per system to the hub). Adding a new 16th system requires 1 new interface (to the hub), not 15 new ones. This is the core mathematical advantage of Hub-and-Spoke.

Q19. (Scenario) A payment processing platform needs to immediately notify four downstream systems (fraud detection, risk scoring, compliance logging, and customer notification) every time a payment is initiated. The payment system must NOT wait for responses from any of these systems — the payment confirmation must happen in milliseconds. Which integration pattern is most appropriate?

A) Point-to-Point — direct calls to each of the four systems
B) Hub-and-Spoke ESB — route the payment event through a central hub
C) API Gateway — single entry point for the downstream systems
D) Event-Driven / Message Broker (Publish-Subscribe) — payment event published; all four systems subscribe independently

Answer: D — Event-Driven/Pub-Sub: The payment system publishes a "PaymentInitiated" event. All four downstream systems subscribe independently and process asynchronously. The payment system does NOT wait for responses (fire-and-forget). This pattern is specifically designed for one-to-many async notification without tight coupling. P2P would require four synchronous calls. API Gateway is for external consumers, not internal async notification.

Q20. What is the key distinction between a Service Contract in SOA and an Architecture Contract in TOGAF?

A) Service Contracts are informal; Architecture Contracts are legally binding
B) A Service Contract defines the technical interface of a specific service (operations, protocol, SLA, authentication); an Architecture Contract is a governance agreement between the architecture team and an implementation project, specifying what must be built and to what standards
C) Architecture Contracts are produced in Phase A; Service Contracts are produced in Phase D
D) They are equivalent concepts used in different contexts

Answer: B — Service Contract (SOA) = technical API definition at the service level (HOW to call a specific service). Architecture Contract (TOGAF Phase F) = governance agreement at the project level (WHAT the project must build and to what architectural standard). They operate at completely different levels. Service Contracts are technical; Architecture Contracts are governance.

Q21. (Scenario) An organization is replacing a monolithic ERP system with a microservices-based platform over 4 years. For the first 18 months, some business units will still use the old ERP while others have been migrated to the new platform. Both must co-exist and interoperate. What TOGAF concept describes these intermediate co-existence states?

A) Work Packages — the migration activities
B) Transition Architectures — stable intermediate states between the Baseline and Target Architectures
C) Architecture Patterns — the reusable integration design
D) Segment Architectures — separate architectures for separate business units

Answer: B — Transition Architectures: formally defined stable states between the AS-IS (monolithic ERP) and the TO-BE (full microservices). Each phase of the migration where old and new co-exist is a Transition Architecture. Defined in Phase E; governed through Phase G. Work Packages are the activities that move from one Transition Architecture to the next.

Q22. (Scenario) The Application/Business Function Matrix for a government agency shows that the "Benefits Calculation" business function is marked as "supported" by four different applications simultaneously. The architecture team notes that all four applications perform the same calculation independently and produce slightly different results. What architectural problem does this reveal and what is the recommended action?

A) A capability gap — the function is not supported; add another application
B) An integration problem — the applications need better interfaces
C) A redundancy problem — multiple applications serving the same function; rationalize using the TIME model to consolidate to one authoritative application
D) A data quality problem — fix the data in each application

Answer: C — The Application/Business Function Matrix reveals redundancies when multiple applications compete for the same function. Four applications doing the same calculation independently, producing different results, is a classic rationalization problem. The action is to use the TIME model to classify each of the four systems (likely some Eliminate, one Invest or Migrate) and consolidate.

Q23. (Scenario) An organization's payroll application is 12 years old but is fully functional, has vendor support until 2028, and processes payroll accurately. However, payroll is not a strategic differentiator for this organization — any modern payroll system would do the same job. The architecture team classifies it in the TIME model. What is the correct classification and recommended action?

A) Invest — payroll is important so keep investing in it
B) Migrate — the system is too old to keep
C) Tolerate — low strategic value, adequate technical health; keep running with no additional investment; revisit when vendor support expires in 2028
D) Eliminate — replace it immediately with a SaaS payroll service

Answer: C — Tolerate: The function is necessary but NOT strategically differentiating; the technology is adequate (vendor support until 2028). The correct action is to keep it running without additional investment, monitor it, and begin migration planning as the 2028 support expiry approaches (which will trigger a Phase H technology trigger). Eliminate requires low value AND the function should stop — but payroll must continue.

Q24. (Scenario) A large retail bank is building a new Open Banking platform that will expose internal banking services to external fintech companies. Authentication, access control, rate limiting, API versioning, and usage analytics for external partners are critical requirements. Which integration pattern best meets the external-facing access requirement?

A) Enterprise Service Bus — centralize all API calls through an internal hub
B) Event-Driven / Pub-Sub — fintech companies subscribe to banking events
C) API Gateway — single managed entry point providing authentication, routing, rate limiting, versioning, and analytics for external consumers
D) Point-to-Point — direct connections between the bank and each fintech company

Answer: C — API Gateway: specifically designed for external consumer access to internal services. It handles authentication, authorization, rate limiting, versioning, and analytics at a single managed point. ESB is for internal enterprise integration, not external partner access. P2P would require a separate connection per fintech company (unmanageable at scale). Pub-Sub is for async event notification, not synchronous API access.

Technology Architecture Questions (Q25–Q30)

Q25. (Scenario) An organization is migrating to cloud. It processes patient health records (subject to strict healthcare data regulations requiring data to remain within national borders). It also runs a public-facing appointment booking website (low sensitivity, high variable traffic). Which cloud deployment models are MOST appropriate for each workload?

A) Both on public cloud — cost-effective
B) Patient records on private cloud (or on-premises); appointment booking on public cloud
C) Patient records on multi-cloud; appointment booking on hybrid
D) Both on private cloud — maximum security

Answer: B — Patient records: Private cloud (or on-premises) for maximum control, compliance, and data sovereignty. Appointment booking: Public cloud for elastic scaling to handle variable demand at low cost. This is a hybrid cloud overall — sensitive workloads in private, non-sensitive in public. Using public for both ignores data sovereignty requirements. Using private for both is unnecessarily expensive for the appointment booking system.

Q26. (Scenario) An organization's customer-facing e-commerce website must handle the failure of any single server without any customer experiencing an error or service interruption. During peak sales events, traffic spikes to 8x normal volume. Which infrastructure pattern best meets both requirements simultaneously?

A) Active-Passive — primary handles peak load; secondary is on standby
B) Cold Standby — reserve infrastructure ready to start
C) Warm Standby — secondary scales up on demand
D) Active-Active with load balancing — all servers simultaneously handle traffic; failure of one server is absorbed by the others; all servers contribute to peak capacity

Answer: D — Active-Active: multiple servers simultaneously handling production traffic through a load balancer. If one fails, others absorb the load — no interruption. All servers are active during peak traffic — providing horizontal scaling. Active-Passive would have brief failover downtime (violates "no interruption") and the passive server doesn't contribute to peak capacity.

Q27. (Scenario) The Architecture Board has approved a new container orchestration platform for use in a limited pilot on two greenfield projects. The approval includes a 12-month evaluation period, after which the Board will decide whether to promote it to a broader standard. Existing projects must continue using the current virtual machine standard. What technology standard category does the container platform have?

A) Mandatory
B) Recommended
C) Emerging
D) Retiring

Answer: C — Emerging: approved for limited/experimental use (pilot projects only); under evaluation by the Architecture Board; not yet proven at enterprise scale. Mandatory = must use. Recommended = should use. Retiring = phase out. A technology "approved for pilot use while being evaluated" is exactly the definition of Emerging.

Q28. (Scenario) During Phase H monitoring, an enterprise architect is alerted that the database platform powering the enterprise data warehouse is scheduled to reach End of Life in 14 months. The vendor has confirmed no further security patches will be issued after that date. The data warehouse contains sensitive customer financial data. How should this be classified in Phase H?

A) Business Trigger — a governance decision is needed
B) Technology Trigger — EOL represents a technology lifecycle event requiring evaluation and likely an architecture change
C) Architecture Trigger — the architecture documentation must be updated
D) This does not require Phase H action — EOL is a normal event handled by IT operations

Answer: B — Technology Trigger: vendor EOL is a technology lifecycle event that triggers Phase H review. Given the sensitivity of the data (customer financial data, security patches stopping), this is a significant risk. Phase H must evaluate whether to respond with a Simplification Change (minor), Incremental Change (loop to Phase E/F to plan migration), or Re-architecting Change (new Phase A cycle). D is wrong — EOL with sensitive data is not routine IT operations; it requires architectural response.

Q29. An organization's Technology Standards Catalog shows four entries for database technology: PostgreSQL 16 (Must use; no exceptions without Board approval), MySQL 8 (Should use; alternatives require justification), CockroachDB (Can use on new projects with Board sign-off; evaluation in progress), Oracle 19c (Do not start new projects; existing systems must migrate by 2027). Which Technology Standard categories do these map to, in order?

A) Required, Preferred, Provisional, Deprecated
B) Mandatory, Recommended, Emerging, Retiring
C) Approved, Suggested, Trial, Sunset
D) Core, Optional, Experimental, Phased Out

Answer: B — TOGAF uses exactly four terms: Mandatory (must use), Recommended (should use), Emerging (can use with approval — being evaluated), Retiring (no new projects; migrate existing). Options A, C, and D use non-TOGAF terminology. B is the only answer using the correct TOGAF terms.

Q30. (Scenario) A technology architect presents two options for a new data analytics platform: (A) deploy on existing on-premises servers to avoid additional cloud costs, or (B) use a public cloud data platform for elastic scaling. The analytics workload has extreme demand variability — quiet for most of the month, then massive spikes during month-end financial close. The business requirement says the platform must handle month-end peaks without degradation. Which option best aligns with TOGAF Technology Architecture principles?

A) Option A — the organization already owns the servers; better asset utilization
B) Option B — technology choices must be driven by application requirements; elastic cloud scaling is the right fit for highly variable workloads
C) Neither — the Architecture Board should decide without architectural recommendation
D) Option A — on-premises always provides better performance than cloud

Answer: B — TOGAF's core principle: Technology decisions are driven by application and business requirements, not by existing infrastructure availability. The analytics workload has extreme variability (month-end spikes) — this is a textbook use case for elastic cloud scaling. Choosing on-premises to "use what we have" is technology-first thinking, which TOGAF explicitly discourages. The Architecture Principle of "Technology Independence" and requirements-driven design both support Option B.

Cross-Domain and Framework Questions (Q31–Q40)

Q31. (Scenario) An architect documents the following: "ADR-031 | Status: Accepted | Context: The organization has 40 enterprise systems needing to integrate. The current 780 point-to-point interfaces are unmaintainable. | Decision: Implement MuleSoft Anypoint Platform as the enterprise integration hub. | Rationale: Reduces connections from 780 to 40. IBM MQ rejected due to higher licensing cost. Custom ESB rejected due to development risk. | Consequences: (+) Centralized monitoring, reduced integration complexity. (-) MuleSoft becomes a critical dependency; hub failure affects all integrations." What type of document is this, and where is it stored?

A) Architecture Contract — stored in the Standards Information Base (Layer 4)
B) Architecture Decision Record (ADR) — stored in the Governance Log (Layer 6)
C) Compliance Assessment — stored in the Architecture Landscape (Layer 3)
D) Requirements Specification — stored in the Reference Library (Layer 5)

Answer: B — This is an ADR — it has all six components (Title/ID, Status, Context, Decision, Rationale, Consequences). ADRs are stored in the Governance Log (Layer 6 of the Architecture Repository), which is the permanent audit trail of all architecture decisions, dispensations, and governance activities.

Q32. (Scenario) An organization uses both TOGAF and ITIL. A TOGAF Architecture Contract has been issued for a new payment processing system. The system has been built and the architecture team has conducted a Phase G Compliance Assessment confirming the system meets all architecture requirements. Before the system can go live in production, what ITIL process must be completed?

A) ITIL Problem Management — root cause analysis of any issues found
B) ITIL Service Level Management — SLA definition and sign-off
C) ITIL Change Management — approval from the Change Advisory Board (CAB) for deploying the change to production
D) ITIL Event Management — production monitoring setup

Answer: C — ITIL Change Management (CAB approval): before any change enters production, ITIL Change Management must assess and approve it. The Architecture Compliance Assessment (TOGAF) confirms architectural correctness; the ITIL Change Record and CAB approval control the production deployment risk. Both must complete before go-live. Phase G (TOGAF) and Change Management (ITIL) are the primary integration point.

Q33. An organization is evaluating TOGAF and the Zachman Framework. The CTO says "we want a structured process to guide our architects through developing architecture — phases, steps, governance." The CDO says "we want a taxonomy to classify and organize all the architecture artifacts our teams produce." Which framework best meets each need?

A) TOGAF for both — it covers both process and classification
B) Zachman for the CTO's need; TOGAF for the CDO's need
C) TOGAF for the CTO's need (ADM process); Zachman for the CDO's need (6x6 classification matrix)
D) Neither — a custom framework is needed

Answer: C — TOGAF = process/method (ADM provides the step-by-step development process the CTO needs). Zachman = classification/ontology (the 6x6 matrix provides the taxonomy for organizing artifacts the CDO needs). They are complementary — use TOGAF to develop, Zachman to classify. B has them backwards.

Q34. (Scenario) An organization using SAFe for software delivery adopts TOGAF. The Agile Release Train (ART) manager says: "Our teams deliver a Program Increment every 10 weeks. We cannot wait 6 months for a full ADM cycle to complete before we can start building." What is the recommended TOGAF-aligned approach?

A) TOGAF cannot be used with Agile; choose one or the other
B) Complete a full ADM cycle before every 10-week PI — Agile teams wait
C) EA maintains an Architecture Runway (architectural decisions made ahead of teams); run abbreviated ADM cycles aligned to PI cadence; teams build within architectural guardrails without waiting for full ADM completion
D) Eliminate architecture governance entirely in Agile contexts

Answer: C — TOGAF Part III explicitly supports Agile contexts. EA maintains the Architecture Runway — designing architectural guardrails ahead of development teams. Abbreviated ADM cycles run in parallel with the PI cadence. Teams work within the established architectural foundations. TOGAF and Agile are complementary at different levels.

Q35. (Scenario) Six months after a new CRM system went live, users report that customer search response times are consistently 6–8 seconds. The Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS) specified a maximum of 2 seconds. The architecture team traces this to under-provisioned database infrastructure. A Phase G Compliance Assessment is conducted. What is the compliance finding, and what are the available options?

A) Conformant — the system is live and functioning
B) Consistent — the system uses the right architecture approach but doesn't meet the performance target
C) Non-conformant — the system fails to meet the ARS performance requirement; options are: (1) provision additional database infrastructure to meet the 2-second requirement, or (2) submit a Dispensation Request to the Architecture Board with a remediation plan
D) Irrelevant — SLA management is an ITIL responsibility, not TOGAF

Answer: C — Non-conformant: the deployed system actively fails to meet the Architecture Requirements Specification (2-second maximum response time). The compliance finding is Non-conformant. Options: (1) remediate — provision the infrastructure to meet the requirement; (2) request Dispensation — formally request an exception from the Architecture Board with a time-bound remediation plan. D is wrong — while ITIL manages SLAs operationally, TOGAF Phase G governs architecture compliance, and a performance requirement in the ARS is an architecture compliance matter.

Q36. (Scenario) An enterprise architect is analyzing the impact of a decision to migrate from an on-premise ERP system to a cloud-based SaaS ERP. Starting from Phase B, trace the cascade. Which sequence correctly describes the order of analysis?

A) Technology Architecture (cloud migration) → Application Architecture (ERP replacement) → Data Architecture (data migration) → Business Architecture (process changes)
B) Business Architecture (what business processes change?) → Data Architecture (what data entities and flows change?) → Application Architecture (what happens to the ERP and its integrations?) → Technology Architecture (what infrastructure changes are needed for cloud SaaS?)
C) Application Architecture → Business Architecture → Technology Architecture → Data Architecture
D) All four can be analyzed simultaneously — there are no dependencies

Answer: B — The Cascade Principle: Business (what processes change with SaaS?) → Data (what entities migrate, what data quality rules change, what governance roles change?) → Application (what replaces the ERP, what integrations change, TIME classification of ERP = Migrate) → Technology (what cloud infrastructure, SaaS model — customer manages only data/config, what data sovereignty requirements for the new cloud SaaS provider?). Always Business first.

Q37. (Scenario) A TOGAF architect discovers that a project team, under schedule pressure, implemented a custom authentication system 18 months ago instead of the Mandatory OAuth 2.0 standard specified in the Architecture Contract. A Dispensation was granted at the time with a commitment to migrate within 12 months. The 12-month deadline has now passed and the migration has not happened. What type of architectural problem does this represent, and in which phase is it managed?

A) A compliance violation in Phase G — the Compliance Assessment team must investigate
B) Architecture Debt in Phase H — an expired Dispensation that was never remediated; must be added to the debt register with a revised remediation plan and escalated to the Architecture Board
C) A governance failure in the Preliminary Phase — the principles need updating
D) A project management failure — outside the scope of TOGAF

Answer: B — This is Architecture Debt (Application Architecture Debt): a Dispensation that was granted with a remediation deadline, the deadline has passed, and the remediation has not happened. Expired dispensations that are never remediated become permanent architecture debt. Phase H Architecture Change Management is responsible for tracking and managing architecture debt. It must be added to the debt register, the risk assessed, and a revised remediation plan developed and approved by the Architecture Board.

Q38. (Scenario) An architect working on Phase C Data Architecture needs to identify who has decision-making authority over the definition, quality standards, and access rules for Customer data — a single executive who is accountable to the Architecture Board for the state of Customer data across the enterprise. Which role is being described, and which framework formally defines it?

A) Data Custodian — TOGAF Part VII (Architecture Governance)
B) Chief Data Officer — the Board of Directors
C) Data Owner — DAMA-DMBOK Data Governance framework (also referenced in TOGAF Architecture)
D) Data Steward — responsible for day-to-day quality management

Answer: C — Data Owner: an executive with decision-making authority and accountability for a specific data domain. Defined in DAMA-DMBOK's Data Governance Knowledge Area and referenced in TOGAF Architecture Governance (they appear in the Actor/Role Catalog and Stakeholder Map). Data Steward handles day-to-day quality implementation (not decision-making authority). CDO handles enterprise data strategy. Data Custodian handles technical storage.

Q39. (Scenario) An organization integrates TOGAF with DAMA-DMBOK. The TOGAF Phase C Data Architecture team has produced a Logical Data Model for the Customer domain, defined data quality requirements (Accuracy > 99%, Completeness = 100% for required fields), and specified that an MDM Centralized Style should be implemented for Customer master data. Which DAMA-DMBOK Knowledge Areas will now take over to implement these architectural decisions operationally?

A) Data Security and Data Storage only
B) Data Modeling & Design; Data Quality; Reference & Master Data — each implements a specific architectural decision from Phase C
C) Data Governance only — one knowledge area manages everything
D) DAMA-DMBOK is not relevant once TOGAF has produced the architecture

Answer: B — TOGAF Phase C produced the WHAT (the architecture): Logical Data Model → DAMA Data Modeling & Design implements it operationally; Data Quality Requirements → DAMA Data Quality implements the quality management program; MDM Centralized Style → DAMA Reference & Master Data implements the MDM solution. TOGAF and DAMA are complementary — TOGAF defines the architectural targets, DAMA implements and operates them.

Q40. (Scenario) At the end of Week 5, an architect is asked to explain why TOGAF organizes architecture into four sequential domains (Business, Data, Application, Technology) rather than letting architects work on all domains simultaneously. What is the BEST explanation?

A) The four domains exist to give separate teams independent work streams — they are parallel and independent
B) The four domains form a service hierarchy: Technology serves Applications, which serve Business needs. The sequential design order ensures that technology decisions are always traceable to business requirements, preventing technology-first thinking and ensuring all IT investment can be justified by business value
C) The four domains are just different names for different types of IT systems — they could be combined
D) TOGAF requires sequential domains because of regulatory compliance requirements

Answer: B — The four domains form a service hierarchy with a deliberate causal direction: Business defines what must be done → Data and Application define what information and systems support it → Technology defines what infrastructure runs those systems. This hierarchy ensures every technology decision is traceable to a business need and prevents technology-first thinking ("we bought this cloud platform, now what do we use it for?"). The domains are distinct (different concerns, different stakeholders, different artifacts) but causally connected in the cascade direction.

Week 5 New Terminology Glossary

These terms are introduced or given full treatment in Week 5. Terms covered in depth in Weeks 1–4 are not repeated here.

Business Architecture Terms

Term Definition
Business Motivation Model (BMM) OMG standard framework connecting business strategy to architecture through Ends (Vision/Goal/Objective) and Means (Mission/Strategy/Tactic), influenced by Influencers
Vision The aspirational future state; most abstract End; qualitative and long-term
Goal Qualitative desired result supporting the Vision; less abstract than Vision
Objective SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) target supporting a Goal; most concrete End
Mission What the organization does — its fundamental activity; most abstract Means
Strategy Broad approach for achieving a specific Goal; less abstract than Mission
Tactic Specific concrete action implementing a Strategy; most concrete Means
Influencer External or internal factor that affects the organization and shapes its Ends and Means (e.g., regulation, competition, culture)
Business Capability What the organization can do at a strategic level; stable; expressed as a noun; does NOT describe how
Business Function A grouping of related activities that produces a specific output; between Capability (strategic) and Process (operational) in abstraction level
Business Process A specific sequential set of activities performed to achieve a defined outcome; describes HOW; modeled in BPMN
Value Chain Porter's model: a high-level model of ALL categories of activities that create value for an organization; generic across organizations in the same industry
Value Stream A specific end-to-end sequence of activities delivering value to a specific stakeholder for a specific outcome; more detailed than Value Chain
BPMN Business Process Model and Notation; standard notation for business processes using events, tasks, gateways, swim lanes, and flows
Pool (BPMN) A BPMN container representing a separate participant (organization, system, external entity)
Lane (BPMN) A subdivision within a Pool representing a role or department
Sequence Flow (BPMN) Solid arrow within a Pool; shows order of activities
Message Flow (BPMN) Dashed arrow between two separate Pools; shows communication between separate participants
Business Footprint Diagram Phase B diagram uniquely tracing business drivers (Goals/Objectives) → Organizational Units → Business Functions → Business Services

Data Architecture Terms

Term Definition
Accuracy Data quality dimension: data correctly represents the real-world entity it describes
Completeness Data quality dimension: all required data is present; no mandatory fields missing
Consistency Data quality dimension: the same data appears the same way across all systems that store it
Timeliness Data quality dimension: data is available when needed and is sufficiently current
Validity Data quality dimension: data conforms to defined formats, ranges, and business rules
Uniqueness Data quality dimension: each real-world entity is represented only once; no duplicates
Canonical Data Model (CDM) A single enterprise-wide standardized format for a data entity used for exchange; reduces N×(N-1)/2 bilateral transformations to N transformations
Master Data Management (MDM) The discipline of defining and managing authoritative records for shared business entities (Customer, Product, Supplier, etc.)
Registry Style (MDM) MDM implementation where a central store holds only cross-references; operational systems retain their own data and remain authoritative
Consolidation Style (MDM) MDM implementation where data is periodically extracted to a central read-only store; operational systems unchanged; central store for reporting only
Coexistence Style (MDM) MDM implementation where central MDM and operational systems are both authoritative in their respective domains; bidirectional synchronization
Centralized Style (MDM) MDM implementation where the central MDM store is the ONLY authority; all systems read master data from the central store only
Data Lineage Historical audit trail of where data originated, all transformations it went through, and where it went; used for compliance and root cause analysis
Data Sovereignty The principle that data is subject to the laws of the country/jurisdiction in which it was collected or processed; drives data residency requirements

Application Architecture Terms

Term Definition
TIME Model Application portfolio classification framework: Tolerate (low value, adequate tech), Invest (high value, good tech), Migrate (high value, poor tech), Eliminate (low value, any tech)
Tolerate TIME category: application has low business value but adequate technical health; keep running without investment; monitor
Invest TIME category: application has high business value and good technical health; actively invest and grow
Migrate TIME category: application has high business value but poor technical health; preserve the function, replace the technology
Eliminate TIME category: application has low business value; decommission; plan the exit
Point-to-Point Integration Integration pattern: direct connections between each pair of systems; N×(N-1)/2 connections for N systems; simple but scales poorly
Hub-and-Spoke / ESB Integration pattern: all systems connect to a central hub/ESB; N connections for N systems; centralized transformation and monitoring
API Gateway Integration pattern: single managed entry point for external consumers; handles auth, rate limiting, versioning, analytics
Event-Driven / Pub-Sub Integration pattern: producers publish events to a message broker; consumers subscribe independently; fully asynchronous and decoupled
Microservices Integration/architecture pattern: application decomposed into small, independently deployable services, each owning its own data
Service Contract (SOA) Technical definition of a service: its operations, input/output data schema, protocol, SLA, and authentication requirements; distinct from TOGAF Architecture Contract
Sunset Planning The formal plan for decommissioning an application: retirement date, replacement, data migration/archival, dependent system changes, contract exit
Application Lifecycle The stages an application passes through: Plan → Acquire/Build → Deploy → Operate → Enhance → Retire

Technology Architecture Terms

Term Definition
IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) Cloud service model: customer manages OS, middleware, application, and data; provider manages hardware, networking, and virtualization
PaaS (Platform as a Service) Cloud service model: customer manages application and data; provider manages OS, runtime, and infrastructure
SaaS (Software as a Service) Cloud service model: customer manages configuration and data only; provider manages everything including the application
Private Cloud Cloud deployment model: infrastructure operated exclusively for one organization; maximum control, security, and compliance; highest cost
Public Cloud Cloud deployment model: shared infrastructure operated by a cloud provider; lowest cost; elastic; least control
Hybrid Cloud Cloud deployment model: combination of private and public cloud with orchestration between them
Multi-Cloud Cloud deployment model: use of multiple public cloud providers simultaneously to avoid single-vendor lock-in
Active-Active (HA) High availability pattern: all servers simultaneously handle production traffic; load balancer distributes requests; near-zero RTO
Active-Passive (HA) High availability pattern: primary server handles all traffic; secondary is on standby; brief failover time on primary failure
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) Maximum acceptable downtime — how long the system can be unavailable during a failure
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) Maximum acceptable data loss — how recent the last good backup must be
Hot Standby (DR) Disaster recovery: full replica running and synchronized in real time; minutes RTO
Warm Standby (DR) Disaster recovery: reduced-scale replica running; scales up on failover; hours RTO
Cold Standby (DR) Disaster recovery: infrastructure exists but not running; must be started and restored; days RTO
Mandatory (Technology Standard) Must be used; no exceptions without Architecture Board approval
Recommended (Technology Standard) Should be used; alternatives require justification
Emerging (Technology Standard) Approved for limited/experimental use while being evaluated; not yet proven at scale
Retiring (Technology Standard) Being phased out; no new projects; existing systems must migrate
Technology Reference Architecture (TRA) Organization-specific application of the TOGAF TRM: maps generic TRM technology service categories to the organization's specific chosen products and their standard category
Technology Debt Accumulated deviations from technology standards: EOL systems, non-standard technology choices, unresolved security vulnerabilities

Cross-Domain and Framework Terms

Term Definition
Cascade Principle Changes flow from Business Architecture → Data and Application Architecture → Technology Architecture; never reversed
Architecture Decision Record (ADR) Formal document capturing a significant architecture decision: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Rationale, Consequences; stored in Governance Log (Layer 6)
Architecture Debt Accumulated deviation from the approved architecture across all four domains; grows through dispensations never remediated, deferred migrations, and permanent workarounds; managed in Phase H
Architecture Runway (SAFe) The existing architectural foundation sufficient to support near-term Agile development; EA maintains it ahead of development teams
Zachman Framework Enterprise architecture classification ontology: a 6×6 matrix organizing artifacts by Interrogative (What/How/Where/Who/When/Why) and Perspective (Executive/Business/Architect/Engineer/Technician/User); a classification tool, not a process
ITIL Information Technology Infrastructure Library; a framework for IT Service Management — how to manage and operate IT services in production
COBIT Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies; a framework for IT Governance and Management — alignment, controls, and audit
Architecture Runway See Architecture Runway (SAFe)

What to Expect in Week 6

Week 6 is the final preparation week before the mock exams in Weeks 7–8. It covers:

  • Full knowledge consolidation: A synthesized review of all five weeks — every critical distinction, every exam trap, and every frequently-tested concept in one place
  • Exam technique: How to read TOGAF scenario questions; elimination strategies; time management for 40 questions in 60 minutes
  • Weak area identification: A structured self-assessment to identify your 2–3 weakest topic areas and targeted review guidance
  • Quick-reference tables: A complete set of comparison tables and decision frameworks for the exam (ADM phases summary, all artifact types, all framework integrations, all governance concepts)
  • 35-question final pre-mock quiz: Exam-weight-accurate question distribution; the final check before you take the full mock exams

Recommended Week 5 → Week 6 transition:

  1. Complete the Day 7 quiz (40 questions)
  2. Score and analyze — identify your weakest topic area by error count
  3. Do 30 minutes of focused re-reading in your weakest area before starting Week 6
  4. Note which question types you consistently get wrong — knowledge gaps or scenario-reading errors? This distinction shapes your Week 6 focus.
